title: “DO NOT GIVE YOUR STRENGTH TO WOMEN”—THE WARNING A MOTHER GAVE A FUTURE KING THAT MEN TODAY ARE STILL IGNORING
paragraphs: “DO NOT GIVE YOUR STRENGTH TO WOMEN”—THE WARNING A MOTHER GAVE A FUTURE KING THAT MEN TODAY ARE STILL IGNORING

Before he ever wore a crown, his mother warned him about the kind of desire that could destroy everything God entrusted to him. But was she warning him about women—or something far more dangerous hiding inside his own heart?
“Give not thy strength unto women, nor thy ways to that which destroyeth kings.” — Proverbs 31:3 (KJV)
There is something heartbreaking about a mother who can see the danger approaching her son before he can see it himself.
She knows his potential.
She remembers the prayers she whispered over him when he was too young to understand them.

She remembers holding him when he was helpless, feeding him when he was hungry, and watching him grow into someone who might one day carry responsibilities far greater than either of them could imagine.
And now she must tell him something he may not want to hear.
Not because she hates women.
Not because she believes love is dangerous.
But because she knows that a man can possess extraordinary strength and still surrender his future to an appetite he refuses to govern.
A man can command armies and still be conquered by his own desires.
He can sit on a throne and still be a slave.
He can have people bowing before him while secretly bowing before something that is destroying him.
And perhaps the most frightening part is this:
He may not recognize his captivity until he has already given away what he can never recover.
That is the weight behind one of the most misunderstood warnings in Proverbs.
“Give not thy strength unto women, nor thy ways to that which destroyeth kings.”
Those words were not spoken by a bitter man recovering from a broken relationship.
They were preserved as the instruction of a mother speaking to her son.
And the identity of that son makes the passage even more intriguing.
Proverbs 31 begins:
“The words of king Lemuel, the prophecy that his mother taught him.” (Proverbs 31:1, KJV)
The Hebrew opens with:
דִּבְרֵי לְמוּאֵל מֶלֶךְ מַשָּׂא אֲשֶׁר־יִסְּרַתּוּ אִמּוֹ
Divrei Lemuel melekh, massa asher yisserattu immo.
In context, the verse introduces the words of King Lemuel, an oracle or weighty saying taught to him by his mother.
The Hebrew word massa (מַשָּׂא) can refer to an oracle or solemn pronouncement. Some interpreters understand it as a reference to Massa, a place or people. The precise identification remains debated.
And Lemuel?
His identity is not established elsewhere in Scripture.
Some traditions associate him with Solomon, but the biblical text does not explicitly identify them as the same person.
We must be careful here.
A powerful sermon should never require us to pretend Scripture says something it does not.
What we know is already extraordinary.
A king remembered his mother's instruction.
And that instruction was considered important enough to be preserved in the Word of God.
Before the warning came the relationship.
Before the correction came the love.
Listen to her words:
“What, my son? and what, the son of my womb? and what, the son of my vows?” (Proverbs 31:2, KJV)
In Hebrew, she repeatedly calls him beri (בְּרִי), meaning “my son.”
There is an intimacy here that English readers can easily miss.
She is not addressing him merely as a ruler.
She is speaking to the child she carried.
The son of her womb.
The son connected to her vows.

The Hebrew expression bar nedarai (בַּר־נְדָרָי) means “son of my vows.” It suggests the deep spiritual seriousness with which she regards her son, though Scripture does not tell us the exact nature of those vows.
She is reminding him that his life matters.
That his decisions matter.
That what he does in private will eventually affect people who never entered his private world.
And then comes the warning.
“Give not thy strength unto women.”
The Hebrew reads:
אַל־תִּתֵּן לַנָּשִׁים חֵילֶךָ
Al-titten lanashim cheilekha.
Literally, the command warns against giving one's chayil to women.
That word matters.
Chayil (חַיִל) can describe strength, capability, wealth, valor, or resources, depending on the context.
It is not limited to physical muscle or sexual energy.
A king's strength includes the resources, judgment, attention, and capacity entrusted to him for governing well.
The warning is about the reckless surrender of those things.
And the next phrase makes the danger clearer:
וּדְרָכֶיךָ לַמְחוֹת מְלָכִין
Uderakhekha lamchot melakhin.
The final expression is difficult Hebrew, but the traditional understanding reflected in the King James Version warns against ways that destroy kings.
The precise wording has been discussed by translators and scholars. The central warning, however, remains unmistakable.
Do not surrender what you have been entrusted with to destructive pursuits.
Do not let appetite overthrow responsibility.
Do not let desire become your ruler.
And do not confuse the ability to obtain something with the wisdom to pursue it.
Because not everything you can have is something you should give your life to.
Now we need to confront something important.
This passage is not teaching that women are the enemy.
That interpretation collapses when we read the entire chapter.
The same Proverbs 31 that warns a king against destructive relationships later celebrates a woman of noble character.
“Who can find a virtuous woman? for her price is far above rubies.” (Proverbs 31:10, KJV)
And the Hebrew word translated “virtuous” is chayil—the same word translated “strength” in verse 3.
Think about that.
The king is warned not to squander his chayil.
Then the chapter praises a woman of chayil.
The same chapter that warns against destructive desire honors a woman whose strength, wisdom, diligence, generosity, and fear of the Lord make her worthy of praise.
That is not a contradiction.
It is a distinction.
The Bible is not warning men against women. It is warning against the destruction that follows when desire is separated from wisdom and faithfulness.
A godly woman is not a threat to a man's calling.
A godly marriage can be one of God's greatest gifts.
But lust, exploitation, adultery, manipulation, and relationships pursued without wisdom can devastate lives.
And the responsibility for a man's choices belongs to the man making them.
It is easy to blame the person who tempted you.
It is harder to admit that something inside you wanted what was being offered.
That is where this passage becomes uncomfortable.
Because some men do not lose their strength in one dramatic moment.
They surrender it little by little.
A conversation they know should have ended.
A message they delete before their wife sees it.
A flirtation they excuse because they feel unappreciated.
A private habit they defend because nobody else knows.
A relationship they keep feeding even though their conscience has been warning them for months.
At first, it feels manageable.
Just a little attention.
Just a little excitement.
Just one more conversation.
But sin rarely introduces itself by announcing the funeral of your future.
It usually begins by offering something that feels like relief.
Relief from loneliness.
Relief from rejection.
Relief from the pressure of always having to be strong.
Relief from a marriage that has become difficult.
Relief from the painful feeling that nobody sees you anymore.
And that is what makes temptation so dangerous.
Sometimes the thing threatening your future initially feels like the thing rescuing you from your present.
But temporary comfort is not always healing.
And being wanted is not the same as being loved.
You can be admired by someone who has no intention of protecting what God has entrusted to you.
You can feel understood by someone who is helping you become dishonest.
You can experience intense attraction while moving farther away from integrity, peace, and obedience to Christ.
And eventually, the question becomes impossible to avoid.
What have you been giving away just to feel something you were afraid you had lost?
Scripture gives us a painful illustration in the life of Samson.
Judges 16 tells us how Samson became entangled with Delilah, who repeatedly sought the secret of his strength.
Samson had been set apart to God from before his birth.
His extraordinary physical strength was connected to God's empowering presence, not to the independent magic of his hair.
Yet he repeatedly placed himself in danger.
He ignored warning signs.
He treated serious spiritual matters carelessly.
And eventually he revealed the secret connected to his Nazirite consecration.
Judges 16:19–20 describes the devastating turning point.
His hair was cut.
His strength departed.
And when he attempted to escape as before, he did not realize that the Lord had departed from him.
That sentence should make every careless heart tremble.
He expected yesterday's strength to carry him through today's disobedience.
But he discovered that presumption is not faith.
And although Samson's story involves betrayal by Delilah, it also exposes Samson's own repeated decisions.
He was not simply a helpless victim of a woman's beauty.
He was a man who repeatedly disregarded danger.
And that is a warning for all of us.
There are consequences that cannot be blamed entirely on the people around us.
Sometimes we knew.
We saw the warning signs.
We heard the conviction.
We recognized the compromise.
And we kept going.
Perhaps that is why this passage feels so personal.
Because you do not need to be a king to have something precious to lose.
Your family may be counting on you.
Your children may be learning what faithfulness looks like by watching your choices.
Your spouse may be trusting you with a heart that has already endured enough pain.
Your church may be relying on your integrity.
Your younger siblings may be following your example.
And even if nobody else sees what you are doing, God does.
Not because He is searching for an excuse to destroy you.
But because nothing about your life is hidden from the One who calls you to walk in truth.
And this warning does not belong to men alone.
Women also face temptations that can distort love, destroy trust, and pull the heart away from God.
The forms may differ.
The underlying struggle is deeply human.
We are all capable of taking a good desire and allowing it to become a destructive master.
That is why the Bible never presents self-control as merely a personality trait for unusually disciplined people.
Galatians 5:22–23 includes temperance, or self-control, among the fruit of the Spirit.
God does not merely tell His people to resist sin through human pride.
He calls them to walk by the Spirit.
Because the deepest problem is not that we lack enough motivational speeches.
It is that our hearts need transformation.
And this is where the story becomes even more searching.
King Lemuel's mother did not stop at relationships.
In Proverbs 31:4–5, she warned rulers against intoxication that could impair their judgment and cause them to forget justice.
Then in verses 8–9, she commanded her son to speak for those who could not speak for themselves and defend the rights of the poor and needy.
Do you see the connection?
The warning about destructive desire was not simply about protecting the king's reputation.
It was about protecting his ability to serve others.
His strength was not given merely for personal pleasure.
His authority carried responsibility.
His decisions affected vulnerable people.
And when a ruler becomes enslaved to his appetites, others often pay the price.
That truth reaches far beyond royal palaces.
A father who sacrifices his family's security to feed a secret addiction is not the only person who suffers.
A mother who abandons honesty for an affair is not the only person affected.
A leader who exchanges integrity for pleasure can wound an entire community.
Sin may begin in private, but its consequences often travel into the lives of people who never consented to the damage.
This is why Scripture treats faithfulness seriously.
Not because God despises human desire.
But because He created us for something greater than being controlled by it.
And then there is Solomon.
We should not pretend that Proverbs 31 identifies Lemuel as Solomon.
It does not.
But Solomon's life provides a separate, sobering biblical example of the danger being described.
First Kings 11 tells us that Solomon loved many foreign women and that his wives turned his heart after other gods.
The issue was not their ethnicity.
The issue was Solomon's disobedience and the idolatry into which his relationships drew him.
God had warned Israel's kings against multiplying wives and turning away from covenant faithfulness (Deuteronomy 17:17).
Solomon possessed extraordinary wisdom.
He had wealth.
He had influence.
He had experienced God's blessing.
Yet wisdom possessed is not always wisdom obeyed.
And there is something deeply tragic about a man who can explain the path of righteousness while walking away from it himself.
Perhaps you know that tension.
You know the verses.
You know the sermons.
You know what God says about holiness, marriage, forgiveness, and truth.
You have encouraged other people to remain faithful.
You have prayed for friends struggling with the very sin you are hiding.
And sometimes the hardest person to confront is the one staring back at you in the mirror.
Because knowing the truth is not the same as surrendering to it.
And religious familiarity is not the same as intimacy with Christ.
But please do not stop reading here.
Because if all we hear from Proverbs 31 is the warning, we may miss the hope that runs through the entire Gospel.
The God who warns us about destruction is also the God who calls sinners to repentance and offers mercy through Jesus Christ.
And no life demonstrates that mercy more beautifully than the life of our Savior.
Think about the woman brought before Jesus in John 8.
She had been caught in adultery.
Her accusers placed her before Him.
They wanted judgment.
They wanted to use her shame as a weapon in their confrontation with Jesus.
And in the middle of that public humiliation stood the only truly sinless person present.
Jesus did not pretend adultery was righteous.
He did not redefine sin to make everyone comfortable.
But neither did He join the crowd's merciless spectacle.
After the accusers departed, Jesus told her:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” (John 8:11, KJV)
Mercy.
And a call to leave sin.
Grace.
And a new direction.
That is the beauty of Christ.
He does not save us by declaring our chains harmless.
He saves us by calling us out of bondage.
He does not offer forgiveness so that we can comfortably remain enslaved.
He offers forgiveness that opens the way to a transformed life.
And perhaps someone reading this has already crossed a line they promised they would never cross.
Perhaps the affair already happened.
Perhaps the marriage has been wounded.
Perhaps the addiction has lasted years.
Perhaps your children have seen a version of you that you desperately wish they could forget.
Perhaps you are sitting in church, smiling at people who have no idea how exhausted you are from carrying a secret.
You love God.
Or at least you remember a time when you did.
But somewhere along the way, you started believing that the damage was too great.
That the years were too wasted.
That the promises were too broken.
That your story had become too ugly for redemption.
Listen carefully.
Your sin may have real consequences.
Some trust may take years to rebuild.
Some relationships may never return to what they once were.
Repentance does not guarantee that every earthly consequence disappears.
And grace must never be used to pressure someone you have harmed into immediate reconciliation.
But the Gospel announces something stronger than despair.
Your failure does not have to become the final authority over your future.
First John 1:9 declares:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Notice what the verse does not say.
It does not say that forgiveness is available only to people whose sins are socially acceptable.
It does not say that cleansing is reserved for people who have never fallen publicly.
It says that God is faithful and just to forgive those who confess their sins.
And the foundation of that forgiveness is not our ability to punish ourselves enough.
It is Jesus Christ.
The Son of God who lived without sin.
Who bore our sins in His body on the cross (1 Peter 2:24).
Who died for our sins according to the Scriptures.
Who was buried.
And who rose again on the third day (1 Corinthians 15:3–4).
This is not cheap encouragement.
This is redemption purchased at an immeasurable cost.
And it means that a person who has surrendered strength to sin can now surrender their life to Christ.
Not to escape responsibility.
But to begin walking in truth.
Not to pretend the past never happened.
But to refuse to let the past remain their master.
Not because they have suddenly become strong enough to save themselves.
But because Jesus is mighty to save.
Think again about Samson.
His story did not end with the moment his strength departed.
In Judges 16:22, after his capture and humiliation, Scripture quietly records:
“Howbeit the hair of his head began to grow again after he was shaven.”
What a sentence.
It does not mean that every consequence was reversed.
Samson remained blind.
He remained captive.
His final act would cost him his life.
But the narrative had not finished.
And when Samson cried out to God in Judges 16:28, the Lord granted him strength for one final act against the Philistines.
His story is not a promise that every fallen believer will recover everything they lost.
It is a reminder that human failure does not place God beyond the reach of a repentant cry.
And even Samson's imperfect story points us toward our need for a greater Deliverer.
One who would not surrender to sin.
One who would not compromise His calling.
One who would remain faithful when everyone around Him failed.
Jesus Christ.
The true and righteous King.
Where earthly kings were corrupted by their appetites, Christ remained obedient to the Father.
Where human rulers neglected the vulnerable, Christ welcomed the weary, the poor, the broken, and the outcast.
Where sinful men used power to serve themselves, Jesus declared that the Son of Man came not to be ministered unto, but to minister, and to give His life a ransom for many (Mark 10:45).
And that is the greatest contrast of all.
Proverbs 31 warns a king not to give away his strength to destructive pursuits.
But Jesus, the King of kings, willingly laid down His life—not in surrender to sin, but in perfect obedience and sacrificial love.
He was not overcome by temptation.
He gave Himself for sinners.
He was not destroyed by an immoral desire.
He went to the cross to redeem people enslaved by sin.
And when He rose again, death itself could not hold Him.
This is why the Christian life is not ultimately about becoming the kind of man who never needs help.
It is about becoming the kind of person who knows where true help comes from.
A man who repents.
A woman who returns to truth.
A husband who chooses faithfulness when nobody is watching.
A wife who refuses to let bitterness rule her heart.
A young person who decides that holiness is worth more than temporary approval.
A fallen believer who stops hiding and comes into the light.
And sometimes that begins with a prayer so simple that pride almost refuses to say it.
“Lord Jesus, I have been giving my heart to things that cannot save me. Forgive me. Teach me to love what is holy. Give me courage to turn away from sin and walk with You.”
Not a performance.
Not a promise that you will never struggle again.
A real surrender.
And if your struggle involves addiction, compulsive behavior, or a relationship that has become destructive, that surrender may also require practical action.
Ending secret communication.
Establishing wise boundaries.
Confessing to a trustworthy and spiritually mature person.
Seeking pastoral counsel or qualified professional support.
Making restitution where appropriate.
Accepting accountability instead of demanding immediate trust.
And if abuse or coercion is involved, seeking safety rather than remaining exposed to harm in the name of reconciliation.
Biblical repentance bears fruit.
It does not merely produce emotional tears.
It changes direction.
And it is never too early to begin walking toward the light.
There is another detail in Proverbs 31 that deserves our attention.
The chapter begins with a mother's instruction and ends with praise for a woman who fears the Lord.
“Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the LORD, she shall be praised.” (Proverbs 31:30, KJV)
Beauty is not condemned as evil.
The warning is that charm can mislead and physical beauty does not last forever.
The enduring foundation of godly character is the fear of the Lord.
And that principle applies to every person.
Do not build your future merely on attraction.
Do not measure someone's worth only by appearance.
Do not confuse popularity with character.
Do not surrender your convictions to keep someone interested in you.
Seek the kind of love that honors truth.
The kind of relationship where faithfulness matters more than excitement.
The kind of character that remains when the compliments stop.
The kind of devotion that leads you closer to Christ rather than teaching you to hide from Him.
Because the greatest relationship you can possess is not one that satisfies every passing desire.
It is one in which love and faithfulness help you walk in the truth.
And if you are single, your life is not incomplete because you do not have a romantic partner.
Your worth is not determined by whether someone chooses you.
Your calling to holiness, love, service, and fellowship with Christ is meaningful right now.
And if you are married, remember that covenant faithfulness is not maintained by romantic feelings alone.
It requires truthfulness, humility, patience, repentance, forgiveness, and deliberate love.
Your spouse is not your savior.
Only Jesus is.
But by His grace, you can learn to love another person with greater integrity and selflessness.
And now, perhaps we can hear Lemuel's mother more clearly.
She was not merely telling her son to avoid scandal.
She was urging him to preserve the capacity to live and lead wisely.
She was reminding him that strength without self-control can become destruction.
That privilege without integrity can become oppression.
That authority without righteousness can become dangerous.
And that a crown cannot protect a heart that refuses correction.
Maybe you are not a king.
But someone needs the strength God has entrusted to you.
Someone needs your honesty.
Someone needs your presence.
Someone needs your prayers.
Someone needs you to stop feeding what is destroying you.
And perhaps the person who needs that most is the one you have been neglecting for years.
Your own soul.
What is receiving the strength, attention, loyalty, and affection that should be governed by your devotion to Jesus Christ?
Is it a secret relationship?
A private addiction?
An appetite for admiration?
A hunger for money?
An obsession with being desired?
A habit of compromising your convictions whenever obedience becomes uncomfortable?
Or perhaps it is not a scandal anyone else can see.
Perhaps it is simply the slow exhaustion of trying to find life everywhere except in the presence of God.
Whatever it is, bring it into the light.
You do not need to announce every private detail to strangers.
But you do need to stop calling darkness harmless.
And you do not need to wait until you feel worthy to approach Christ.
Come to Him in repentance and faith.
Come with the truth.
Come with the wreckage.
Come with the questions.
Come with the grief of realizing how much time you have wasted.
Come with the desire to begin again.
Because the cross is not a monument to the strength of people who never failed.
It is the place where the sinless Savior gave Himself for people who could never save themselves.
And His empty tomb is the announcement that sin and death do not have the final word over those who belong to Him.
This is why we keep proclaiming the Gospel.
Not to build an audience around human personalities.
Not to sell the illusion that following Jesus makes life painless.
But because there are people quietly losing battles nobody knows they are fighting.
There are fathers who need to come home spiritually.
There are mothers carrying grief they have never spoken aloud.
There are young people confusing attention with love.
There are marriages that need truth and repentance.
There are believers who have stopped opening their Bibles because shame convinced them God no longer wants to hear from them.
And there are people who have never truly understood what Jesus accomplished at the cross.
You do not have to expose painful private details publicly. Even a few honest words can become the beginning of encouragement and prayer within a community of believers.
And if you have experienced Christ's mercy after a season of compromise, your testimony may remind someone that repentance and restoration are still possible.
Do not underestimate the power of a truthful testimony that points away from self and toward Jesus.
If this article brought someone to mind, consider sharing it directly with them in love, not accusation.
We also want to invite you into something deeper.
These resources are part of our desire to make biblical nourishment, encouragement, and practical discipleship more accessible.
Scripture teaches:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.” (2 Corinthians 9:7, KJV)
That is the heart with which we invite you.
Not guilt.
Not pressure.
Not a transaction with God.
But willing generosity in response to His goodness.
But the greatest gift we can offer is not merchandise.
It is the faithful proclamation of the Gospel that points people to Jesus Christ.
Because the Gospel is not for sale.
The mercy of Jesus cannot be purchased.
And no monthly payment can make someone more deserving of God's love.
We support Gospel ministry because Christ is worthy—not because our financial support earns His favor.
That distinction matters.
And so does your soul.
One day, the things that once competed so fiercely for your attention will lose their power to impress you.
The applause will fade.
The temptation will pass.
The beauty that once captivated you will change with time.
The possessions you worked so hard to accumulate will belong to someone else.
Even the strongest human body will eventually grow weak.
But the Word of the Lord endures forever.
And the life built upon Jesus Christ rests on a foundation stronger than passing desire.
So remember the mother who warned a future king.
Remember Samson, who discovered that strength can be squandered.
Remember Solomon, whose wisdom did not excuse his disobedience.
Remember the woman standing before Jesus, where mercy met the command to leave sin.
And above all, remember the Savior who refused every temptation, carried our sins to the cross, and rose victorious from the grave.
You may have surrendered too much to something that never truly loved you.
You may have lost years that you cannot recover.
You may have wounds to acknowledge, wrongs to repair, and consequences to face.
But if you are still breathing, the call to repent and believe the Gospel still stands before you.
Do not give another day to the lie that your past must be your permanent identity.
Turn to Christ.
Tell the truth.
Receive His mercy.
Walk in obedience.
And let the life that once testified to your failure become a testimony to the transforming grace of God.
Because the most tragic thing is not that you once gave your strength to what was destroying you. It is to hear the voice of the Savior calling you home—and still refuse to let go.
